Pepper___Bacterial_spot.scientific_name: Xanthomonas spp. (e.g., Xanthomonas euvesicatoria / X. vesicatoria)
key_symptoms: Small, water-soaked irregular spots on leaves that may become angular
Lesions on fruit (scabby, raised, dark lesions)
Leaf yellowing and premature defoliation under severe infection
diagnostic_clues: Water-soaked lesions in humid conditions
Brown/black lesions on fruit with greasy appearance
Often worse when overhead irrigation is used
transmission: Spread by splashing water (rain, overhead irrigation)
cultural_controls: Use pathogen-free seed and transplants
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation to reduce splash
Remove and destroy infected plant debris; rotate crops
Sanitize tools and hands
biological_controls: Biocontrols are limited; focus on cultural + tolerant varieties where available
chemical_controls_examples: Use in integrated program; effectiveness can decline due to resistance
prevention: Implement sanitation and cover/spacing to reduce humidity
Pepper___Bacterial_spot.notes: Bacterial diseases often respond best to prevention and sanitation; chemical control is supplementary.

key_symptoms: No disease symptoms; leaves, stems, and fruit appear normal
diagnostic_clues: Absence of lesions, chlorosis, necrosis or vector presence
management: Standard good agronomic practices; monitor regularly for pests/diseases
Pepper___healthy.notes: Keep good records and collect labelled examples of any new symptoms for diagnosis.

key_symptoms: Dark, concentric-ring lesions (target-like) on older leaves
Lower leaves affected first, may cause defoliation
Lesions on stems and tuber skin in severe cases
diagnostic_clues: Concentric rings within lesions (classic 'target' spot)
Symptoms typically start on older foliage during warm, wet weather
transmission: Overwinters in crop debris, cull piles
Spores dispersed by wind and splashing water
cultural_controls: Crop rotation and burying/destroying infected debris
Use certified seed potatoes
Avoid excessive nitrogen which increases lush growth
biological_controls: Experimental; common strategy is IPM combining cultural and chemical
chemical_controls_examples: Some systemic fungicides (strobilurins, DMIs) are used in rotation

key_symptoms: Water-soaked, dark lesions on leaves that expand rapidly
White fuzzy sporulation on leaf underside in humid conditions
Rapid collapse of foliage; infected tubers show brownish rot under skin
diagnostic_clues: Very rapid disease spread in cool, wet conditions
White fuzzy sporulation at lesion margins under high humidity
transmission: Can be spread by infected seed tubers
cultural_controls: Use certified seed tubers; remove infected plants and cull tubers
Improve airflow, avoid overhead irrigation
Crop rotation and avoid planting near volunteer potatoes
biological_controls: Limited; focus on resistant varieties and chemical programs
chemical_controls_examples: Oomycete-active fungicides (phenylamides like metalaxyl/mefenoxam historically; phosphonates/phosphites; other oomycete-specific actives)
Use recommended local fungicide programs and rotate modes of action
prevention: Use resistant varieties where available; strict seed certification
Rapid detection & removal to limit outbreaks

key_symptoms: No disease lesions or discoloration on foliage or tubers
management: Maintain good seed, rotation, irrigation, and soil health practices

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.scientific_name: Xanthomonas spp. (e.g., X. euvesicatoria / X. vesicatoria)
key_symptoms: Small, water-soaked, scabby or angular spots on leaves
Lesions on fruit (dark, raised, scabby)
Defoliation and reduced yield under severe pressure
diagnostic_clues: Water-soaked appearance initially; greasy lesions on fruit
Often associated with warm, wet weather and overhead irrigation
cultural_controls: Use disease-free seed and transplants
Avoid overhead irrigation; remove infected debris
Sanitize tools and limit plant-to-plant contact
chemical_controls_examples: Integrated program to reduce resistance risk
prevention: Certified clean seed; resistant/tolerant varieties if available

key_symptoms: Dark lesions with concentric rings on lower older leaves (target spot)
Defoliation starting from the bottom upward
Lesions may appear on stems and fruit in heavy infections
diagnostic_clues: Classic concentric ring pattern inside lesions
Worse in warm, humid conditions and where crop debris persists
transmission: Spores survive in crop residue; spread by wind and splash
cultural_controls: Rotate crops and remove/bury crop debris
Avoid excess nitrogen; use proper spacing for airflow
chemical_controls_examples: Protectant fungicides (chlorothalonil) and systemic fungicides in rotation
prevention: Resistant varieties when available; sanitation and rotation

key_symptoms: Water-soaked, dark lesions on leaves and stems; rapid collapse
White-gray sporulation present on lesion margins in humid conditions
Fruit may show firm, greasy lesions; rapid spread under cool-wet weather
diagnostic_clues: Rapid progression, white sporulation on underside in humid weather
Associated with cool, wet conditions and windblown spores
transmission: Windborne sporangia; infected seed or volunteer plants
cultural_controls: Use certified seed, remove infected plants, improve airflow
Avoid planting near infected fields or volunteer potatoes
chemical_controls_examples: Oomycete-targeting fungicides (e.g., mefenoxam/metalaxyl historically; phosphonates/phosphites; other recommended actives) used per local guidance
prevention: Rapid detection and removal, resistant varieties where available
recommended_references: PlantVillage, university extension pages (NC State, etc.)

key_symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety spots on underside of leaves
Yellowing of upper leaf surface opposite the moldy underside spots
Defoliation in severe cases
diagnostic_clues: Velvety olive to brown sporulation on the underside of leaves
Symptoms worse in warm, humid greenhouse conditions
transmission: Conidia spread via air, water, or contaminated transplants
cultural_controls: Improve ventilation and spacing; avoid overhead watering
Remove infected leaves and debris; use resistant varieties if available
chemical_controls_examples: Fungicide protectants and appropriate systemic fungicides as recommended locally
prevention: Sanitation and good greenhouse/housing practices; choose clean transplants

Tomato___Mosaic_Virus.scientific_name: Mosaic viruses (e.g., Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV), Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV))
primary_hosts: Tomato, many solanaceous species and other hosts (virus-dependent)
key_symptoms: Mottled light-and-dark green mosaic pattern on leaves
Leaf distortion, stunting, smaller fruit
Symptoms depend on virus strain and host
diagnostic_clues: Characteristic mosaic pattern; often uneven growth
Viruses often persist in seed, contaminated tools, and on hands
transmission: Mechanically via sap on hands, tools, handling; some viruses seed-borne or vectored by insects depending on virus
cultural_controls: Use virus-free seed and transplants; sanitation of tools and hands
Remove infected plants promptly to reduce spread
biological_controls: No chemical cures for plant viruses; focus on prevention and vector control
prevention: Certified clean seed, resistant varieties (if available), strict sanitation

key_symptoms: Many small, circular lesions with dark borders and pale centers on lower leaves
Heavy defoliation of lower canopy under wet conditions
Typically begins on older leaves
diagnostic_clues: Small roughly circular spots often with tiny black fruiting bodies visible with magnification
Worse in humid, wet weather
transmission: Fungal spores splash-dispersed from infected debris; survives in residue
cultural_controls: Remove crop residue, rotate crops, increase spacing for airflow
Avoid overhead irrigation; mulch soil to reduce splash
chemical_controls_examples: Protectant fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) and appropriate systemic actives rotated to prevent resistance
prevention: Sanitation and reducing leaf wetness; resistant varieties where available

key_symptoms: Fine stippling/speckling on leaves (chlorotic points)
Webbing on heavily infested plants; bronzing of foliage
Reduced vigor and yield if heavy infestation
diagnostic_clues: Tiny mites visible with hand lens and fine webbing in advanced infestations
Symptoms often worse in hot, dry conditions
transmission: Mites move by crawling or carried on wind, equipment, transplants
cultural_controls: Maintain adequate irrigation (reduces stress that favors mites), encourage natural predators (predatory mites, ladybugs)
Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticides that kill beneficial predators
chemical_controls_examples: Miticides (use selective products and follow resistance management guidance)
prevention: Monitor with sticky cards and plant inspections; encourage biological controls

primary_hosts: Tomato and many other plants (some strains are host-specific)
key_symptoms: Circular to irregular lesions with concentric rings (target-like) on leaves
Leaf blighting under favorable conditions
diagnostic_clues: Target-like concentric lesion patterns; check host and local disease reports
transmission: Windborne spores and splash; survives in crop residues
cultural_controls: Crop sanitation and residue removal; rotate hosts
Avoid overhead irrigation and reduce leaf wetness
chemical_controls_examples: Fungicide protectants and appropriate systemic fungicides where recommended
recommended_references: Plant pathology and university extension resources

Tomato___YellowLeaf_Curl_Virus.scientific_name: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV) — a begomovirus
key_symptoms: Severe leaf yellowing and upward curling of new leaves
Stunted plants and reduced yield; small, distorted fruit
diagnostic_clues: Rapid onset of curling and yellowing on new growth; presence of whiteflies on plant
Often severe in regions where whitefly vectors are abundant
transmission: Transmitted by the whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) in a persistent manner
Can be introduced on infected seedlings
cultural_controls: Control whitefly populations (screens, insect-proof greenhouses, reflective mulches), remove infected plants
Use virus-free seedlings and resistant varieties when available
biological_controls: Conservation of natural enemies of whiteflies can help reduce vector pressure
chemical_controls_examples: Insecticidal control of whiteflies (use IPM principles; rotate modes of action to limit resistance)
prevention: Use resistant varieties where available; implement vector management and sanitation
recommended_references: PlantVillage and extension publications on TYLCV and whitefly management

key_symptoms: No visible disease; normal leaf shape, color and fruit development
management: Maintain sanitation, monitoring, and use certified seed/transplants
